title: A novel approach to resilience in cold-work applications: experimental comparison of the as-built mechanical properties of high-alloy 1.2709, high-alloy 1.4125 and low-alloy 1.7228 produced using PFB-LB/M
abstract: Abstract Additive manufacturing (AM), and in particular laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), is increasingly being used in tooling applications. Commonly used steels such as 1.2709 and 1.2344 are commercially available, while other grades such as 1.2379 cannot be processed easily with PBF-LB/M due to limited powder availability and poor weldability. In addition, tool steels are highly alloyed and often contain conflict-related raw materials that critically affect long-term material availability. To address this challenge, this study presents a comparative material selection method based on a key performance indicator that evaluates the alloy compositions in terms of their supply chain resilience and suitability for tooling applications. In this context, resilience is primarily defined by combining the chemical composition with the achievable hardness. Based on this, low-alloy steel 1.7228 was identified as a promising replacement for high-alloy cold work steels. A powder made from 1.7228 was produced specifically, suitable process parameters were developed using correlation analysis and mechanical properties in the as-built state were determined and compared with other available tooling steels for PBF-LB/M (1.2709, 1.4125). The results show that 1.7228 has a higher average impact energy of 45 J than 1.4125 with 4 J. In addition, 1.7228 achieves a higher tensile strength (1,547 MPa) than other materials and higher hardness values (477 HV50) than 1.2709 (340 HV50). These experimental results show that 1.7228 enables material substitution for application-specific scenarios, maintaining or exceeding mechanical performance, which supports the sustainable use of scarce raw materials and the need for heat treatments.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The demand for high-strength and high-hardness steels for cold work applications remains high. These properties are particularly important in order to counteract the increasing cost pressure in this industry [ 1 ]. Conventional cold work tool steels typically achieve hardness values above 480 HV [ 1 ], but require complex multi-stage heat treatments and a high content of alloying elements [ 1 ,  2 ]. These factors limit their applicability in PBF-LB/M, where crack susceptibility while welding [ 3 ], and material availability are significant constraints. Alloying elements such as tungsten (W), nickel (Ni), and cobalt (Co) are used to adjust the properties [ 2 ] but are often associated with fluctuating prices, limited availability, and ethical concerns due to their mining in conflict and war-torn regions. Many of those mining countries are therefore classified as  High Risk  [ 4 ]. In addition to the risk, that trading in these minerals could finance armed groups and thus conflicts, mining may also be associated with slavery, child labor and negative environmental impacts [ 5 ]. For most parts of the world, it is therefore advisable to substitute limited-available materials not only from the perspective of supply chain resilience, but also for reasons of long-term sustainability and ethical standards [ 4 ,  6 ]. Especially W is classified as a  Conflict Mineral  [ 7 ]. In the wake of global regulations, laws such as the  Dodd-Frank Act  [ 8 ] in the US and similar European directives such as the  EU Conflict Minerals Regulation  [ 9 ] have attempted to monitor the trade of such materials in order to minimize their negative impact.

Parallel to these challenges, PBF-LB/M has emerged as a promising manufacturing process for tools due to its design freedom and potential for functional integration, such as internal cooling channels [ 10 ]. However, only a few steels are suitable and available for this process. The number of steels available in 2020 was still only around ten different alloys [ 11 ]. In comparison, according to the  World Steel Association , there are over 3,500 different conventional grades of steel [ 12 ]. Initially well-weldable materials, 1.4404 or 1.2709 [ 3 ] with as built hardness values of ≈ 370 HV [ 13 ] were processed. Over time it is also possible to reliably process difficult-to-weld materials. Some of those are high-speed steel 1.3343 with as-built hardness values of 775 HV but a W-content of 6.2% [ 14 ] or moderately weldable tool steels, such as 1.2344 [ 15 ]. Recent research has also focused on qualifying low-alloy steels like 1.7131 (as-built hardness ≈ 550 HV) [ 3 ], 1.6511 (as-built hardness ≈ 490 HV) [ 16 ], 1.7225 (as-built hardness ≈ 500 HV) [ 17 ].

The innovative approach of this work involves the targeted selection of materials that are suited for PBF-LB/M, without resorting to critical alloying elements and the necessity of heat treatments while still ensuring sufficient mechanical performance. This is done by developing the  Resilience Factor  as a key performance indicator for steels and by conducting an experimental comparison of the mechanical properties of three steels: high-alloy 1.2709 typically used for molds, high-alloy 1.4125 typically used for cutting tools, and low-alloy 1.7228 suitable for forming tools. These three materials intend to cover different levels of alloying levels, as well as different assessments of weldability and thus processability. The focus of the experimental approach is the evaluation of the as-built hardness, strength and impact toughness values as well as the resilience of the materials in order to make a conscious and sustainable contribution to reducing dependence on critical raw materials. It is assumed that 1.7228 has superior impact toughness and strength values compared with the other alloys while showing similar or also improved hardness in the as-built state. This enables a sustainable material replacement and the reduction in necessary heat treatments.

sections.heading: Resilience factor and material selection
paragraphs: Throughout this study, risk factors were based on Germany’s political guidance. Germany is the seventh largest steel producer worldwide, has limited domestic resources, and, for that reason, is particularly dependent on imports [ 18 ]. In a 2018 report, alloying elements were divided into three groups based on a weighted country risk and country concentration [ 19 ]. A comparison of risk assessments over the years, which is shown in Table  1 , makes it clear that there has been little change in assessments of supply chain resilience, which demonstrates the need for conscious use of materials and material substitution. Table 1 Main alloying elements for tooling steels and their classification into risk factor groups in 2018, 2021, 2024 and their final assessment Element Risk factor 2018 [ 19 ] Risk factor 2021 [ 20 ] Risk factor 2024 [ 4 ] Final risk factor Carbon (C) 3 3 n.a 3 Cobalt (Co) 3 3 3 3 Chromium (Cr) 2 3 2 2 Manganese (Mn) 2 2 n.a 2 Molybdenum (Mo) 2 2 1 2 Nickel (Ni) 1 1 3 3 Silicon (Si) n.a 3 2 3 Tungsten (W) 3 3 2 3 Vanadium (V) 3 3 1 3 Legend: 1: critical, 2: highly critical, 3: extremely critical

A high RF indicates that a more resilient supply chain can be assumed for the future. A low RF indicates that the material may be more difficult to procure in the future, which can mean no—to-limited availability or high price levels, because raw material prices have shown significant volatility predominantly from 2017 to 2023 [ 21 ]. The final risk factor was based on the  K-Nearest Neighbors  algorithm. This approach was chosen because other statistical parameters, such as the median or the average, could have led to a distortion of the group assignment. With this algorithm the risk factor that occurred most frequently within the three data points was selected as the final factor. Only Ni was also assigned the largest factor, as current studies on supply chain resilience indicate that this material could face significant problems in the future. This is partly because around two-thirds of annual Ni output is used in steel production [ 22 ]. It is also because important future technologies such as battery production are increasingly reliant on it and demand for it could triple by 2030 [ 23 ].

Examples of selected materials, also in comparison to their achievable hardness, which is particularly important in punching applications, are shown in Fig.  1 . The minimum requirement and common hardness values were extracted from a profitable material recommendation [ 1 ]. Special literature (e.g. World of Steel [ 2 ], Steel Handbook [ 24 ], VDI 3388 [ 25 ]) dealing with cold work steels was selected in advance to initially test the method. Furthermore, potential and promising steels were pre-selected in collaboration with a supplier of raw materials. As can be seen, achieving high hardness (> 58 HRC) is usually associated with a RF of < 50%, particularly in the range of materials available for the PBF-LB/M process. Only material 1.4125 with the brand name  THOR44  from  Asgaard Metals  achieves a RF of > 60% [ 26 ]. If these values are compared with materials that are not available in powder form, it becomes clear that there is still potential for material substitution. Even tough other materials for tooling applications have a high resilience factor of > 80%, such as 1.2510 and 1.2550, they still rely on a low W-content (0.7% / 2.2%) or 1.2767 on a Ni-content (4.3%). Other materials do exhibit a high RF, but are only to a limited extent suitable for PBF-LB/M due to their increased C-content. The processability was of decisive importance for the choice of material, as the available equipment did not have the option of pre-heating the build platform. Thus, the material 1.2370, 1.2379 or 1.2601 were considered non-processable in the present case [ 14 ]. However, what also stands out is that low-alloyed steels, such as 1.7227 offer advantages, as they have a high RF of around 90% while also achieving hardness values of > 59 HRC [ 25 ]. Fig. 1 Resilience factor vs. achievable hardness for pre-selected tooling steels

Based on this investigation and in consultation with a raw material supplier, 1.7228, which is closest to the displayed material 1.7227, was selected. It has a resilience level of 91% and can achieve hardness values of > 60 HRC [ 27 ] which exceeds 1.7227. The material was specially gas atomized by  Nanoval GmbH & Co. KG . In order to show the contrasts between the individual gradations between the RF and to be able to compare the mechanical characteristics in the as-built condition, the material 1.4125 (THOR44) from  Asgaard Metals  and tool steel 1.2709 from  LPW Technology Ltd.  were also processed. This choice of material also allows to determine the influence of C-content on as-built hardness values, which is primarily added for hardness in the majority of tool steels [ 2 ,  28 ]. Furthermore, the material 1.4125 is one of the only materials with achievable hardness values of > 60 HRC without the use of W. The material 1.2709 was selected due to its sound data base for comparison purposes.

sections.heading: Process parameter development
paragraphs: Prior to processing, all materials were characterized in accordance with VDI 3405 [ 29 ]. A detailed description of the results is included in the appendix. In order to develop parameters for the 1.7228, which has not yet been processed in this form, preliminary tests were carried out with an  AL3D-Metall-250—50  originally from  Alpha Laser GmbH  using Argon 4.6 as a protective gas. Unlike the standard model, the available system has a fiber laser with 250 W CW, a wavelength of 1,070 nm, and a focus diameter of 50 µm [ 30 ]. In accordance with VDI 3405, cube-shaped test specimens with edge lengths of 10 × 10 × 10 mm 3  were produced [ 29 ]. An initial guess for the parameters was based on previous publications on the similar material 1.7225 and is compiled in Table  2 . Table 2 Available parameter sets for 1.7225 for an initial guess as first parameter indication for 1.7228 Laser power [W] Scan velocity [mm/s] Hatch distance [µm] Layer thickness [µm] Relative density [%] References 250 1,300 60 30  > 99.00 [ 31 ] 250 867 90 40 – [ 32 ] 275 800 120 30  > 99.60 [ 33 ]

After each build job with nine specimens, the samples were measured for their relative density (RD) in accordance with DIN EN ISO 3369 using Archimedes’ principle. In addition, the samples were tested for hardness using a  ZHU250  device from  Zwick Roell . The hardness was measured in Vickers (HV50) in accordance with EN ISO 6507. In order to generate improved parameter sets between the test runs correlation analyses ((Pearson correlation coefficient [ 34 ]) were conducted and are shown in Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 1.7228: Pearson correlation coefficient of the machine parameters on relative density and hardness  a  relative density over line energy  b  hardness over line energy  c

The primary focus on those analyses were on RD and the hardness an according to the correlation analysis, the line energy had the greatest influence on the target variable in each case. In the case of the PBF-LB/M process, the line energy is calculated by dividing the laser power by the scanning speed [ 35 ]. The volume rate, which can be seen in Fig.  2 a, is the multiplication of the scan velocity, the hatch distance and the layer thickness. The volume energy density is determined by dividing the laser power by the volume rate [ 13 ]. Within five iteration cycles, parameters with a RD of > 99.9% were extracted using a laser power of 200 W and a scan velocity of 900 mm/s. As can be seen in Fig.  2 b and c, RD values the highest hardness values can be achieved with a line energy between 0.20 and 0.25 J/mm. Nevertheless, the experiments were continued in order to further fill the data room and better understand correlations. All data sets are attached in the appendix. Explicit representations can be provided upon reasonable request. In addition to the density and hardness values, the surface properties were also measured and the parameters optimized. A  Keyence VK-X1000  laser scanning microscope was used for this purpose. For 1.4125 the parameter development procedure was designed analogously, whereby parameter sets from the literature could be used [ 36 ]. For this material a laser power of 158 W and a scan velocity of 590 mm/s is used. A parameter set similar to the one of the machine manufacturers for 1.2709 a with given laser power of 155 W and a scan velocity of 600 mm/s was used. The developed and available parameter sets with the achieved physical and mechanical properties are compiled in Table  3 . A layer thickness of 30 µm was used for all materials and the contour was scanned before the hatch. sections.heading: Experimental details
paragraphs: Since the  AL3D-Metall-250—50  does not have a sufficient build envelope for the production of standard-confirm tensile test specimens (TTS) and charpy pendulum impact test specimens (CPITS), the manufacturing of those was carried out with an  AL3D-Metall-200—100 , the larger system from  Alpha Laser GmbH  which is equipped with a 100 mm diameter build plate. With regard to the machine transferability of the process parameters, nine cubes were manufactured in advance for 1.4125 and 1.7228, which yielded in equivalent RD values. Therefore, the same process parameters developed and tested with the smaller machine were used for further tests for all materials. Nine vertical TTS form A and CPITS with V-notches were produced for each material. The arrangement was carried out in accordance with VDI 3405. The dimensions of the specimens were taken from DIN 50125 and DIN 148—1. A diameter of d 0  6.0 mm was selected for the TTS. Due to restrictions in terms of overall build height, the clamping length (h) was reduced from 25.0 mm to 16.0 mm but therefore the clamping diameter (d 1 ) was increased from 8.0 mm to 12.0 mm. The samples were manufactured near net shape with an additional allowance and machined in order to comply with the required dimensions and surface tolerances. The positioning and dimensions of the TTS are listed in Table  4 . The numbering of the test specimens also corresponds to the order of melting. This ensures that scanning takes place in the opposite direction to the flow of the protective gas and therefore that powder bed contaminations by spatter or other by-products produced during the melting of the powder are kept to a minimum [ 37 ]. Table 4 Positioning and dimensions of the manufactured tensile test specimens

A similar procedure was chosen for the production of the CPITS. The V-notch was already pre-manufactured during the additive build-up, but was then re-milled to ensure the required geometric accuracies and surface tolerances. The positioning and dimensions are summarized in Table  5 . When positioning the CPITS, an azimuth angle of 45° was selected in accordance with VDI 3405 avoiding longer edges transverse to the recoating direction and thus avoiding the risk of recoater collisions or uneven powder layers. The pure examination of test specimens produced in build direction aims to determine the minimum achievable mechanical properties. Table 5 Positioning and dimensions of the manufactured chapry pendulum impact test specimens

sections.heading: Relative density and as-build surface quality
paragraphs: The results for the RD measured according to Archimedes’ principle are summarized in Fig.  3  and Fig.  4 . To verify these measurements, which are based on the whole test specimen’s geometry, light-micrographs were taken in selected planes of two specimens per material and sample type and evaluated using image analysis. This analysis was again performed in accordance with VDI 3405. The TTS samples were measured for its RD prior to destructive testing while the CPITS were measured following the destructive testing. Both sample halves (lower and upper) were subsequently measured individually in order to be able to provide an assessment, of whether there was a change in the RD values over the build height. The micrographic results as well as the build direction (BD) for the TTS specimens are shown in Fig.  5 ,  6  and  7  and the ones for the CPITS specimens in Figs.  8 ,  9  and  10 . In the case of the CPITS, the surface roughness was determined prior to post-processing. The surface opposite the numbering was selected as the measuring surface. Measurements were taken in BD and the results are shown in Fig.  11 Fig. 3 Summary of the relative density values of the manufactured tensile test specimens determined using archimedes’ principle Fig. 4 Light micrograph sections (unetched) of tensile test specimens of no. 4. and 8. of the material 1.2709 Fig. 5 Light micrograph sections (unetched) of tensile test specimens of no. 3. and 9. of the material 1.4125 Fig. 6 Light micrograph sections (unetched) of tensile test specimens of no. 2. and 7. of the material 1.7228 Fig. 7 Summary of the relative density values of the manufactured charpy Pendulum impact test specimens determined using archimedes’ principle Fig. 8 Light micrograph sections (unetched) of charpy pendulum impact test specimens of no. 4. and 8. of the material 1.2709 Fig. 9 Light micrograph sections (unetched) of charpy pendulum impact test specimens of no. 3. and 9. of the material 1.4125 Fig. 10 Light micrograph sections (unetched) of charpy pendulum impact test specimens of no. 2. and 7. of the material 1.7228 Fig. 11 Representation of the surface roughness values achieved for the charpy pendulum impact test specimens

For 1.4125 and 1.7228 all samples exhibit RD values of > 99% across the entire build platform. Minor spherical microdefects (< 0.01 mm) can be observed in both the lower and upper areas of the samples, which indicate a slightly increased energy input. Macro cracks were discovered in one sample (tensile test specimen No. 3 / Fig.  5 ) of 1.4125. This may be due to local process fluctuations at the beginning of the manufacturing process. However, since no similar defects can be observed in any other sample, it can be assumed that this does not represent a general problem. Further investigation on this will still be carried out to verify that this is really not a general problem, since cracks in other samples cannot be diffidently excluded at this point. Defects in the interface of hatch and contour scanning were detected in the samples of 1.7228.

However, it is clear that the transfer of the process parameters for material 1.2709 did not work. Both the density measurement yielded in RD values of <  < 99.0%. The defects are clearly attributable to a  Lack of Fusion  (LOF) problem, with some of the pores > 0.3 mm. This may be due to a non-homogeneous powder bed [ 38 ] or a too little energy input [ 39 ]. Due to the larger machine bed and longer recoating paths, the influence of the primarily non-spherical particle shape may have been more pronounced than with the smaller machine and built plates [ 40 ]. Furthermore, the inability to transfer process parameters between the two machines for this material may be the reason for the poor results.

The different results between the two methods for determining RD values for all three materials are consistent with previous findings in the literature. Archimedes’ principle considers the entire volume of the sample, whereas image analysis only considers a cross-section. Therefore, the image analysis of metallographic specimens tends to shows higher RD values [ 41 ]. However, the uneven distribution of the samples in the microscopic images confirms the generally good density values. In addition, the differences in the results regarding density measurement for the CPITS of 1.2709 correspond with results from previous publications. While the Archimedes density measurement method is highly accurate across all density levels, the results obtained using light micrographs show slightly too high a value at low density levels. However, the advantage of the microscopic images is that they allow the type of internal pores to be qualified [ 41 ].

With regard to surface roughness, it can be noted that scanning the contour before hatching resulted in a significant improvement in surface roughness compared to the preliminary tests. In addition, sample No. 4 shows the lowest roughness values for 1.4125 and 1.7228. Specimen No. 7 shows the lowest roughness value for the material 1.2709. Overall, it is striking that the specimen on the left of the build plate (No. 2, No. 4, No. 7) in most cases exhibit significantly better surface roughness than samples on the right. To illustrate this more clearly, the results are shown in Fig.  11 . This might be explainable by the protective gas flow, in particular its flow speed distribution. However, a detailed investigation will not be discussed here. It should be noted, however, that significantly better values were achieved for material 1.2709 (R z  ≈ 60µm) compared to the specifications in VDI 3405 (R z  100 µm).

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: The hardness measurement was performed on the CPITS, as the sample geometries provided better measurement surfaces, after the post-processing. The force of 50 kp was applied within 6 s and then held for 12 s according to DIN EN ISO 6507—1. Similar to the density, one measurement was performed in the upper area and one in the lower area in order to identify changes across the build height. The results are shown in Fig.  12 . Fig. 12 Summary of the hardness values (hv50) of the charpy pendulum impacts test specimens

It can be stated that hardness values in accordance with the literature could be achieved for 1.2709 and 1.4125 (1.2709: 370 HV [ 27 ], 1.4125: 479 HV [ 29 ]). No. 1 of 1.4125 has a significantly higher value than all other samples. This can be explained due its tendency work hardening during post-processing. The cutting parameters had to be tested for this material first and were apparently not yet optimal. Due to the plastic deformation of the test specimen instead of chip removal as a result of a too high feed rate, the surface hardness may have increased. For material 1.7228, it is noticeable that the originally relatively high hardness values of > 500 HV50 could no longer be achieved. It is also noticeable for this material that all samples in the lower area achieved a significantly higher hardness value than those in the upper area. One explanation for this could be that the continuous and prolonged heat input in the lower layers results in process-related heat treatment. Alternatively, the effect of the build plate on the cooling rate could have let to lower regions cool down faster. However, further investigations are necessary to confirm these statements. When comparing the material 1.7228 with the more common 1.7225, only minor differences in hardness are observed despite variations in C-content. With a hardness in the range of 400—450 HV50, 1.7225 falls within the same range as the parameter study conducted in this work for 1.7228 [ 31 ,  32 ]. When compared with other low-alloy steels, 1.7228 still has one of the highest hardness values achievable especially when alloying elements such as W and Ni are avoided [ 42 ].

sections.heading: Tensile test
paragraphs: A  multiXtens II HP  device from  Zwick Roell  was used to perform the tensile tests. The samples were dimensioned to be sufficiently long so that the existing extensometer could be used in order to measure the change in length until the sample broke [ 43 ]. The results for the achieved yield strength (YS) values and the ultimate tensile strength values (UTS) are shown in Fig.  13 . The associated stress–strain-curves are shown in Fig.  14 . In most cases, the altered clamping dimensions did not have any negative impact on the test procedure. However, minor problems arose for sample No. 8 and 9 of 1.4125 as can be seen from their stress–strain curves in Fig.  14 . With No. 7, the clamping force was not sufficient meaning that it was not possible to successfully complete the test. Fig. 13 Summary of yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength values Fig. 14 Stress–strain curves

For 1.2709 and 1.4125 YS values and UTS values corresponding to those given in the literature or according to the data sheet could be achieved (achieved mean value for 1.2709: YS 943 MPa; UTS 1,121 MPa [ 13 ] and 1.4125: YS 910 MPa; UTS 1,217 MPa [ 26 ]). These results are particularly surprising for 1.2709, as significantly poorer strength values were expected due to the LOF pores [ 44 ]. What stands out is that a significantly lower elongation at break (EAB) was measured for all materials (achieved mean values for 1.2709: 1.26%., 1.4125: 1.39%, 1.7228: 4.66%). This might be explained by the specimen’s dimension and by the test in as-built condition. In his dissertation, Bültmann describes that in tensile tests with smaller specimen diameters, the EAB also decreases, while the actual strength values are independent of the specimen thickness [ 45 ]. However, another explanation for the significantly lower EAB can be found in the residual porosity at 1.4125 and the significant porosity at 1.2709. Du et al. [ 46 ] have shown that EAB is drastically reduced, especially if LOF pores are present. Furthermore, it was already discussed in chapter 4.2 that cracks in the 1.4125 samples cannot be ruled out in general. It is therefore also possible that cracks in the test area (L c ) led to a reduction in mechanical properties. A correlation between cracks and reduced properties in samples manufactured using PBF-LB/M has already been demonstrated for other materials [ 47 ].

Compared to conventional material, 1.7228 achieved strength values with a mean UTS value of 1,547 MPa in the as-built condition that can be assigned to strength class I [ 27 ], with the exception of EAB (4.7%) which can also be due to the residual porosity. The porosity shown in Fig.  6  in the surface area of the sample may have led to an additional mechanical weak point. This porosity, which is most likely due to an excessive contour-to-hatch-distance, is located in the area of the allowance that was added for post-processing. These areas may have been exposed during post-processing. In his publication, Wawrzyniak [ 48 ] et al. describes a significant reduction in strength values and EAB with increasing porosity. When likewise comparing the as-built values with the available data for 1.7225, 1.7228 stands out for its higher strength. Compared to other low-alloy steels, 1.7228 usually exhibits significantly better or at least comparable strength values in its as-built state. In some cases, 1.7228 even exceeds the strength values of other materials in their heat-treated state. An overview of this is shown in Table  6 . However, the values for the other materials were not verified within the scope of this work and are based on publications. sections.heading: Charpy pendulum impact test
paragraphs: A testing device developed in-house by the  Materials Technology Laboratory  was available for conducting the CPIT. The values determined for the three materials are shown in Fig.  15 Fig. 15 Summary of values from the charpy pendulum impact test

The impact toughness determined for 1.2709 with a mean value of 13.28 J are significantly lower than those specified by other powder manufacturers.  Sandvik Osprey  states that, the impact toughness of its  Osprey®18Ni300  in the as-built condition is between 63 and 108 J. Lower values, such as those determined in the present case, are only achieved after a heat treatment process [ 49 ]. The reduced values can be explained by the poor RD results and the orientation of the samples (horizontal) [ 39 ]. Even lower impact toughness values were achieved for material 1.4125 with a mean value of 4.06 J. However, unlike for 1.2709, no literature references could be found for samples produced using PBF-LB/M. For conventional materials, impact toughness values of 9 J—22 J are specified in the hardened state (650 HV) [ 50 ,  51 ]. To check whether the lower values were due to the horizontal installation direction, two further horizontal samples were produced. However, these two samples also only achieved values in the range of 5 J, which means that the low values cannot be attributed to the BD. One explanation could be the micro-pores and the associated reduction in load-bearing capacity under impact loads. However, further tests need to be carried out to verify this statement, as the strength values for static loads were not negatively affected in any way.

1.7228 showed the highest impact toughness with a mean value of 45.06 J, despite the fact that, in most cases, it also achieved the highest hardness values. This corresponds with the literature on the similar material 1.7225 [ 17 ]. This may be due to the fact that the material exhibits lower brittleness, as illustrated by the EAB if it is compared to the 1.4125 specimens. A detailed comparison with material 1.2709 cannot be made due to the poor RD. Also, for this material, the remaining gas pores may have slightly impaired the mechanical characteristics achieved. However, if the impact toughness values are compared to the specifications for the standard material (> 27 J at 400—490 HV [ 27 ]), a significantly better performance of the PBF-LB/M samples can be seen, as well as in a direct comparison with 1.7225. With an impact energy of approximately 5 – 40 J, the 1.7225 alloy also falls below the values for 1.7228 [ 17 ,  52 ]. Consequently, superior mechanical properties can be confirmed.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook
paragraphs: To evaluate and compare steel in terms of their supply chain resilience, a key performance indicator  Resilience Factor  has been introduced, which is based on the specific chemical composition (CC) of a material. Taking a Germany-centric perspective as an example, this contribution assumes the fact that certain elements, such as Co and W, are often mined in politically semi-stable regions and elements such as Ni will be in significantly higher demand in the future. On this basis, three materials with varying resilience factors and hardness promises were selected, processed using PBF-LB/M, and mechanically characterized. The key findings are: Even though C is one of the most important alloying elements for the hardenability of steels, there is no continuous trend between the C-content and the resulting hardness of components in the as-built condition across different materials. Furthermore, no significant change could be detected between hardness and increased C-content under otherwise identical CC conditions (1.7218 / 1.7225 / 1.7228), as is the case with other materials [ 53 ]. When comparing materials with similar CC (1.7218 / 1.7225 / 1.7228), it becomes apparent that an increased C-content leads to an improvement in performance in terms of strength values (UTS + 14% / + 20%) and impact toughness (+ 12%) The selection of materials shows that comparable or better mechanical properties can also be achieved in the as-built condition with the more resilient steel 1.7228 than with high-alloyed tool steels 1.4125 and 1.2709. This means that a material substitution in general is possible. Even materials that are considered difficult to weld can be processed using PBF-LB/M without the need for preheating. This generally results in the same or even higher performance values in terms of component load capacity. This may be due to reduced internal stresses resulting from the smaller size of the used machines and the lower energy input during melting (line energy 1.7225: 0.3 J/mm, 1.7228: 0.22 J/mm). However, this statement needs to be verified [ 54 ].

Further work is needed to establish this possibility of material substitution. This includes, among other things: Further investigations on cracking mechanisms for 1.4125 to prove that the found cracks are not a general problem. Review and comparison of the mechanical properties of 1.4125 and 1.7228 in the heat-treated state Evaluation of the resulting microstructure to provide additional insights and to verify the previous direct comparison between 1.7225 and 1.7228 as well as the influence of the C-content of the hardening mechanism. Evaluation of the residual stresses of 1.7228 in order to confirm the statement regarding the crack susceptibility. An AI-supported approach to expand the parameter window for material 1.7228 and, if necessary, further increase the as-built mechanical properties. Creation of real-world applications for material substitution to test the performance of resilient materials in comparison to currently in use materials. Especially in light of the tendency of 1.4125 to work hardening and the resulting applications Extent the definition of the resilience factor to make it a fit also for non-steel materials or for applications where a minimum Cr-content for corrosion resistance is needed.
